modules.title: Introduction to Kubernetes
modules.content:
Learning Objectives
Ee module complete ayyaka meeru:

   ●​    Kubernetes ante enti ani ardham chesukuntaru.
   ●​    Enduku Kubernetes use chestaro telustundi.
   ●​    Docker ki Kubernetes ki difference telustundi.
   ●​    Kubernetes use cases gurinchi basic knowledge vastundi.

Topic 1: What is Kubernetes?
Definition
Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform used to deploy,
manage, scale, and monitor containerized applications automatically.

Simple ga cheppali ante:

        Kubernetes is a tool that manages Docker containers automatically.

Easy Explanation
Oka company lo 100 Docker containers run avuthunnayi ani anukondi.

Problems:

    ●​   Oka container crash ayindi.
    ●​   Traffic ekkuva vachindi.
    ●​   Konni containers stop ayyayi.
    ●​   New version deploy cheyyali.

Ivanni manually manage cheyyadam chala kashtam.

Kubernetes ee panulanni automatic ga chestundi.

Real-Life Example
🏢 Oka hotel lo manager untadu.
Hotel staff:

    ●​   Chef
    ●​   Waiter
    ●​   Cleaner
    ●​   Cashier

Manager em chestadu?

    ●​ Work assign chestadu.
    ●​ Staff absent ayithe replacement arrange chestadu.
    ●​ Customers ekkuva unte extra staff pettadu.

Alage Kubernetes kuda containers ni manage chestundi.

Why is Kubernetes Called K8s?
"Kubernetes" ane word lo:

K + 8 letters + s

Kabatti short form:

K8s

Main Responsibilities of Kubernetes
    ●​   Deploy applications
    ●​   Manage containers
    ●​   Restart failed containers
    ●​   Scale applications
    ●​   Load balancing
    ●​   Automatic updates
    ●​   Monitor application health

Example Scenario
Oka shopping website undi.

Festival sale start ayindi.

Suddenly:

    ●​ 10,000 users website open chesaru.

Without Kubernetes:

    ●​ Website slow avvachu.
    ●​ Server crash avvachu.

With Kubernetes:

    ●​ Automatic ga extra containers create chestundi.
    ●​ Load ni divide chestundi.
    ●​ Website smooth ga run avuthundi.

Advantages
    ●​   Open Source
    ●​   Free to use
    ●​   Automatic Scaling
    ●​   Self-Healing
    ●​   High Availability
    ●​   Easy Deployment
    ●​   Cloud Support
    ●​   Secure

Disadvantages
   ●​ Beginners ki konchem difficult.
   ●​ Setup konchem complex.
   ●​ Small projects ki avasaram lekapovachu.

Important Keywords
    Term                  Meaning

 Container      Application package

 Cluster        Group of machines

 Pod            Smallest unit in
                Kubernetes

 Node           Machine in the cluster

 Deployment     Runs and manages Pods

Interview Questions
Q1. What is Kubernetes?

Answer:​
 Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform used to deploy, manage,
scale, and monitor containerized applications automatically.

Q2. Why is Kubernetes called K8s?

Answer:​
Because there are 8 letters between K and S in the word "Kubernetes".

Summary
   ●​   Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform.
   ●​   It manages Docker containers automatically.
   ●​   It provides scaling, self-healing, and load balancing.
   ●​   It is widely used in cloud-native applications.

modules.title: Kubernetes Architecture
modules.content:
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

    ●​    Understand Kubernetes Architecture.
    ●​    Identify Control Plane and Worker Node components.
    ●​    Explain the role of each Kubernetes component.
    ●​    Understand how a request flows inside a Kubernetes cluster.

2.1 What is Kubernetes Architecture?
Definition
Kubernetes Architecture is the overall structure of a Kubernetes cluster. It explains how
different components work together to deploy and manage containerized applications.

In simple words:

         Kubernetes Architecture is the blueprint that shows how Kubernetes
         manages applications.

Real-Time Example
Imagine a college.

    ●​ Principal → Gives instructions
    ●​ Teachers → Manage classrooms
    ●​ Students → Attend classes

Similarly,

    ●​ Control Plane (Master Node) → Gives instructions
    ●​ Worker Nodes → Run applications
    ●​ Pods → Actual applications

2.2 Kubernetes Cluster
A Kubernetes Cluster is a group of computers (called nodes) that work together to run
applications.

A cluster mainly contains:

   ●​ Control Plane
   ●​ One or more Worker Nodes

Simple Diagram

             Kubernetes Cluster

     +-----------------------------+

     |       Control Plane           |

     +-----------------------------+

         /        |          \

         /        |          \

+-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+

| Worker Node | | Worker Node | | Worker Node |

+-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+

     |            |              |

   Pods               Pods               Pods

Image Suggestion: Search "Kubernetes Architecture Diagram" and insert it below this
topic.

2.3 Control Plane (Master Node)
The Control Plane is the brain of Kubernetes.

It manages the entire cluster.

Responsibilities

   ●​ Receives user requests.

   ●​   Decides where applications should run.
   ●​   Monitors cluster health.
   ●​   Restarts failed applications.
   ●​   Stores cluster information.

Components

   ●​   API Server
   ●​   Scheduler
   ●​   Controller Manager
   ●​   etcd

2.4 Worker Node
A Worker Node is the machine where applications actually run.

Each Worker Node contains:

   ●​   Kubelet
   ●​   Kube Proxy
   ●​   Container Runtime
   ●​   Pods

Responsibilities

   ●​   Runs containers.
   ●​   Communicates with the Control Plane.
   ●​   Reports node status.
   ●​   Executes application workloads.

2.5 API Server
The API Server is the entry point of Kubernetes.

Whenever you run a command like:

kubectl get pods

the request first goes to the API Server.

Responsibilities

    ●​   Accepts requests.
    ●​   Validates requests.
    ●​   Updates cluster information.
    ●​   Communicates with other components.

2.6 etcd
etcd is Kubernetes' database.

It stores all cluster information.

Examples:

    ●​   Pods
    ●​   Deployments
    ●​   Nodes
    ●​   Secrets
    ●​   ConfigMaps

Without etcd, Kubernetes cannot remember the cluster state.

2.7 Scheduler
The Scheduler decides where a Pod should run.

Example:

Suppose there are 3 Worker Nodes.

Worker 1 → Busy ❌
Worker 2 → Busy ❌

Worker 3 → Free ✅

The Scheduler selects Worker 3.

2.8 Controller Manager

The Controller Manager checks whether the cluster is working correctly.

Example:

If a Deployment should have 3 Pods, but one Pod crashes, the Controller Manager
automatically creates a new Pod.

This feature is called Self-Healing.

2.9 Kubelet
Kubelet runs on every Worker Node.

Responsibilities:

   ●​   Talks to the API Server.
   ●​   Starts Pods.
   ●​   Stops Pods.
   ●​   Reports Node status.

Think of Kubelet as the manager of a Worker Node.

2.10 Kube Proxy
Kube Proxy manages networking inside Kubernetes.

Responsibilities:

   ●​ Routes traffic to Pods.
   ●​ Load balances requests.
   ●​ Enables communication between services.

2.11 Container Runtime
The Container Runtime is responsible for running containers.

Examples:

   ●​ containerd

   ●​ CRI-O

Earlier, Docker was commonly used directly, but modern Kubernetes typically uses
containerd or other CRI-compatible runtimes.

2.12 How Kubernetes Works (Workflow)
   1.​ Developer deploys an application using kubectl.
   2.​ API Server receives the request.
   3.​ Scheduler selects the best Worker Node.
   4.​ Controller Manager monitors the deployment.
   5.​ Kubelet starts the Pod on the Worker Node.
   6.​ Kube Proxy routes traffic to the Pod.
   7.​ etcd stores the cluster state.

Summary
   ●​   Kubernetes uses a Control Plane and Worker Nodes.
   ●​   The Control Plane manages the cluster.
   ●​   Worker Nodes run applications.
   ●​   API Server is the entry point.
   ●​   Scheduler selects the best node.
   ●​   Controller Manager maintains the desired state.
   ●​   Kubelet manages Pods on each Worker Node.
   ●​   Kube Proxy handles networking.
   ●​   etcd stores cluster information.

Interview Questions
1. What is Kubernetes Architecture?

Answer: Kubernetes Architecture is the structure of a Kubernetes cluster consisting of a
Control Plane and Worker Nodes that work together to manage containerized applications.

2. What is the role of the API Server?

Answer: It is the entry point of Kubernetes. It receives and validates requests and
communicates with all other Kubernetes components.

3. What is etcd?

Answer: etcd is a distributed key-value database that stores the complete state and
configuration of the Kubernetes cluster.

4. What is the role of the Scheduler?

Answer: The Scheduler selects the most suitable Worker Node to run newly created Pods.

5. What is the difference between the Control Plane and a Worker Node?

                Control Plane                                    Worker Node

 Manages the cluster                             Runs applications

 Makes decisions                                 Executes workloads

 Contains API Server, Scheduler, Controller      Contains Kubelet, Kube Proxy, Container
 Manager, etcd                                   Runtime, Pods

modules.title: Installing Kubernetes
modules.content:
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Understand the requirements for installing Kubernetes.
   ●​   Install Docker, kubectl, and Minikube.
   ●​   Create a local Kubernetes cluster.
   ●​   Verify the installation.
   ●​   Deploy your first application.

3.1 Introduction
Before learning Kubernetes concepts like Pods and Deployments, we need a Kubernetes
cluster.

For learning purposes, we use Minikube, which creates a single-node Kubernetes cluster on
your computer.

To create this cluster, we need:

   ●​ Docker (Container Runtime)
   ●​ kubectl (Command Line Tool)
   ●​ Minikube (Local Kubernetes Cluster)

3.2 Prerequisites
Before installing Kubernetes, make sure your system meets these requirements.

   Requirement                     Minimum

 Operating           Windows 10/11, Linux, macOS
 System

 RAM                 4 GB (8 GB Recommended)

 CPU                 Dual Core or Higher

 Storage             20 GB Free Space

 Internet            Required for Downloads

3.3 Tools Required
   Tool                  Purpose

 Docker     Runs containers

 kubectl    Communicates with Kubernetes

 Minikube   Creates a local Kubernetes
            cluster

3.4 Installing Docker
What is Docker?
Docker is a platform used to create and run containers.

Kubernetes manages containers, but it first needs a container runtime like Docker (or
containerd).

Installation Steps

   1.​ Download Docker Desktop from the official Docker website.
   2.​ Install Docker.
   3.​ Restart your computer.
   4.​ Open Docker Desktop.
   5.​ Wait until Docker starts successfully.

Verify Docker Installation

Open Command Prompt or Terminal and run:

docker --version

Expected Output:

Docker version 28.x.x

Check if Docker is running:

docker ps

If no error appears, Docker is working correctly.

3.5 Installing kubectl
What is kubectl?
kubectl is the command-line tool used to communicate with a Kubernetes cluster.

It allows you to:

    ●​   Create Pods
    ●​   Delete Pods
    ●​   View Nodes
    ●​   Deploy Applications
    ●​   Check Logs

Installation Steps

    1.​ Download kubectl from the official Kubernetes website.
    2.​ Install it.
    3.​ Add it to the system PATH (if required).

Verify Installation

Run:

kubectl version --client

Expected Output:

Client Version: v1.xx.x

3.6 Installing Minikube
What is Minikube?
Minikube is a lightweight Kubernetes distribution used for learning and development.

Instead of creating multiple servers, Minikube creates a single-node Kubernetes cluster
on your computer.

Installation Steps

    1.​ Download Minikube.
    2.​ Install it.
    3.​ Open Terminal or Command Prompt.

Verify installation:

minikube version

Expected Output:

minikube version: v1.xx.x

3.7 Starting a Kubernetes Cluster
Start Minikube using:

minikube start

This command:

    ●​   Creates a Kubernetes cluster.
    ●​   Starts the Control Plane.
    ●​   Starts the Worker Node.
    ●​   Configures kubectl automatically.

The first startup may take a few minutes.

3.8 Checking Cluster Status
Check Minikube status:

minikube status

Example Output:

host: Running

kubelet: Running

apiserver: Running

kubeconfig: Configured

This means the cluster is running successfully.

3.9 Verify Kubernetes Installation
Check cluster information:

kubectl cluster-info

Check nodes:

kubectl get nodes

Example Output:

NAME        STATUS      ROLES          AGE

minikube    Ready      control-plane 5m

If the node status is Ready, your installation is successful.

3.10 Your First Kubernetes Application
Run an Nginx application:

kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx

Check deployment:

kubectl get deployments

Check Pods:

kubectl get pods

You should see an Nginx Pod in the Running state.

3.11 Useful Minikube Commands
Start Cluster

minikube start

Stop Cluster

minikube stop

Delete Cluster

minikube delete

Open Dashboard

minikube dashboard

3.12 Common kubectl Commands
View Nodes

kubectl get nodes

View Pods

kubectl get pods

View Deployments

kubectl get deployments

View Services

kubectl get services

Describe a Pod

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

Delete a Pod

kubectl delete pod <pod-name>

3.13 Common Installation Errors
Error 1: Docker is not running

Reason: Docker Desktop is closed.

Solution: Start Docker Desktop and try again.

Error 2: kubectl command not found

Reason: kubectl is not installed or not added to PATH.

Solution: Install kubectl and verify the PATH configuration.

Error 3: Minikube failed to start

Reason: Virtualization is disabled or Docker is not running.

Solution: Enable virtualization in BIOS and ensure Docker is running.

3.14 Best Practices
   ●​   Install the latest stable versions.
   ●​   Ensure Docker is running before starting Minikube.
   ●​   Use kubectl get nodes to verify cluster status.
   ●​   Stop Minikube when not in use to save system resources.
   ●​   Practice using kubectl commands regularly.

Interview Questions
1. What is Minikube?

Answer: Minikube is a tool that creates a single-node Kubernetes cluster on a local machine
for learning and development.

2. What is kubectl?

Answer: kubectl is the command-line interface used to communicate with and manage a
Kubernetes cluster.

3. Why do we need Docker before installing Minikube?

Answer: Docker provides the container runtime needed by Minikube to create and run the
Kubernetes cluster.

4. Which command starts a Kubernetes cluster?

minikube start

5. Which command checks available nodes?

kubectl get nodes

modules.title: Pods – The Smallest Unit in
modules.content:
Kubernetes
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​    Understand what a Pod is.
   ●​    Explain why Pods are used in Kubernetes.
   ●​    Create and manage Pods.
   ●​    Understand Pod lifecycle.
   ●​    Write a simple Pod YAML file.
   ●​    Use basic Pod commands.

4.1 Introduction to Pods
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes.

In simple words,

        A Pod is a wrapper that contains one or more containers.

Kubernetes does not create Docker containers directly. Instead, it creates Pods, and Pods
run the containers.

4.2 Why Do We Need Pods?
Suppose you have an Nginx application.

Without Kubernetes:

    ●​ Docker directly runs the Nginx container.

With Kubernetes:

    ●​ Kubernetes creates a Pod.
    ●​ The Pod contains the Nginx container.
    ●​ The Pod manages the container.

This makes application management easier.

4.3 Real-Time Example
Imagine you order food online.

    ●​ The food is placed inside a delivery box.
    ●​ The delivery person carries the box, not the food directly.

Similarly:

    ●​ Container = Food
    ●​ Pod = Delivery Box
    ●​ Kubernetes = Delivery Person

Kubernetes manages the Pod, not the container directly.

4.4 Pod Architecture
             Kubernetes Cluster

                  |

              Worker Node

                  |

             +---------------+

            |    Pod        |

            |---------------|

            | Nginx Container|

            +---------------+

Image Suggestion: Search "Kubernetes Pod Architecture" and insert the diagram here.

4.5 Components of a Pod
A Pod may contain:

   ●​ One or more containers
   ●​ Shared Network
   ●​ Shared Storage (Volumes)

Shared Network

Containers inside the same Pod share:

   ●​ IP Address
   ●​ Port Space

Example:

Container A can communicate with Container B using localhost.

Shared Storage

Containers inside a Pod can share files using Volumes.

4.6 Single Container Pod
Most Pods contain only one container.

Example:

Pod

└── Nginx Container

This is the most common deployment in Kubernetes.

4.7 Multi-Container Pod
A Pod can also contain multiple containers.

Example:

Pod

├── Main Application

└── Logging Container

The second container supports the main application.

This is called the Sidecar Pattern.

4.8 Pod Lifecycle
A Pod goes through different phases.

1. Pending

The Pod has been created but is waiting to be scheduled.

2. Running

The Pod is running successfully.

3. Succeeded

The Pod completed its task successfully.

4. Failed

The Pod stopped because of an error.

5. Unknown

Kubernetes cannot determine the Pod status.

4.9 Creating a Pod Using Command
Create an Nginx Pod:

kubectl run nginx --image=nginx

Check Pods:

kubectl get pods

Example Output:

NAME        READY STATUS       RESTARTS AGE

nginx      1/1   Running   0      2m

4.10 Pod YAML File
Instead of using commands, Kubernetes recommends YAML files.

Example:

apiVersion: v1

kind: Pod

metadata:

 name: nginx-pod

spec:

 containers:

 - name: nginx

  image: nginx

  ports:

  - containerPort: 80

Save the file as:

pod.yaml

Create the Pod:

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

4.11 Important Pod Commands
View Pods

kubectl get pods

Detailed Information

kubectl describe pod nginx-pod

View Logs

kubectl logs nginx-pod

Delete Pod

kubectl delete pod nginx-pod

Edit Pod

kubectl edit pod nginx-pod

4.12 Pod vs Container
                    Pod                   Container

 Kubernetes Object               Docker Object

Can contain one or more                Contains application code
containers

Has its own IP Address                 Uses Pod network

Managed by Kubernetes                  Managed by Container Runtime

4.13 Advantages of Pods
  ●​   Easy to manage
  ●​   Supports shared networking
  ●​   Supports shared storage
  ●​   Fast deployment
  ●​   High availability with Kubernetes controllers

4.14 Limitations of Pods
  ●​ Pods are temporary (ephemeral).
  ●​ If a Pod is deleted, its IP address changes when recreated.
  ●​ Pods are not designed for permanent storage.

4.15 Best Practices
  ●​   Use one main container per Pod whenever possible.
  ●​   Use YAML files instead of imperative commands.
  ●​   Use meaningful Pod names.
  ●​   Monitor Pod status regularly.
  ●​   Use Deployments to manage Pods in production.

Interview Questions
1. What is a Pod?

Answer:​
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes that contains one or more containers.

2. Can a Pod contain multiple containers?

Answer:​
 Yes. Multiple containers can run inside the same Pod and share the same network and
storage.

3. Which command creates a Pod?

kubectl run nginx --image=nginx

4. Which command displays all Pods?

kubectl get pods

5. Why are YAML files preferred?

Answer:​
 YAML files provide a declarative way to define Kubernetes resources. They are reusable,
version-controllable, and easier to maintain than manual commands.

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Create an Nginx Pod using the command line.

Task 2

Create the same Pod using a YAML file.

Task 3

View the Pod details.

Task 4

Check the Pod logs.

Task 5

Delete the Pod

modules.title: Kubernetes Services &
modules.content:
Networking
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​    Understand what a Kubernetes Service is.
   ●​    Learn why Services are required.
   ●​    Differentiate between Service types.
   ●​    Expose applications to users.
   ●​    Understand basic Kubernetes networking.

5.1 What is a Kubernetes Service?
A Service is a Kubernetes object that provides a stable network endpoint to access one or
more Pods.

Simple Definition

        A Kubernetes Service is used to expose Pods so that users or other applications
        can access them.

5.2 Why Do We Need Services?
Pods are temporary (ephemeral).

If a Pod crashes or is recreated:

    ●​ A new Pod gets a new IP address.
    ●​ Applications using the old IP will fail.

A Service solves this problem by providing a fixed IP and DNS name.

Example

Without Service:

User → Pod (10.0.0.5)

Pod crashes

New Pod → 10.0.0.8

User still tries 10.0.0.5   ❌
With Service:

User → Service → Pod

Pod changes

User → Same Service → New Pod         ✅
The Service automatically forwards traffic to the new Pod.

5.3 How Does a Service Work?
          User

            |

         Kubernetes Service

            |

   -------------------------

   |        |           |

  Pod 1         Pod 2          Pod 3

The Service distributes requests among all available Pods.

5.4 Types of Kubernetes Services
Kubernetes provides four main Service types:

   1.​ ClusterIP
   2.​ NodePort
   3.​ LoadBalancer
   4.​ ExternalName

5.5 ClusterIP
ClusterIP is the default Service type.

Features

   ●​ Accessible only inside the Kubernetes cluster.
   ●​ Used for communication between applications inside the cluster.

Example

Frontend → Backend API

The frontend accesses the backend using a ClusterIP Service.

5.6 NodePort
A NodePort exposes the application outside the cluster using a port on every Worker Node.

Example

http://192.168.1.10:30080

Advantages:

   ●​ Easy for testing
   ●​ Accessible from a browser

Disadvantages:

   ●​ Not recommended for production.

5.7 LoadBalancer
A LoadBalancer Service is mainly used in cloud platforms like AWS, Azure, and GCP.

It creates an external IP address.

Advantages:

   ●​ Public access
   ●​ High availability
   ●​ Automatic traffic distribution

Example:

https://myapp.example.com

5.8 ExternalName
An ExternalName Service maps a Kubernetes Service to an external DNS name.

Example:

database.company.com

Instead of creating a new database inside Kubernetes, applications can access the external
database.

5.9 Service YAML Example

apiVersion: v1

kind: Service

metadata:

 name: nginx-service

spec:

 selector:

  app: nginx

 ports:

 - protocol: TCP

  port: 80

  targetPort: 80

 type: ClusterIP

Create the Service:

kubectl apply -f service.yaml

5.10 Useful Service Commands
View Services

kubectl get services

Describe Service

kubectl describe service nginx-service

Delete Service

kubectl delete service nginx-service

View Endpoints

kubectl get endpoints

5.11 Kubernetes Networking Basics
In Kubernetes:

   ●​   Every Pod gets its own IP address.
   ●​   Pods can communicate with each other.
   ●​   Services provide a stable endpoint.
   ●​   DNS helps applications communicate using names instead of IP addresses.

Example:

Instead of:

10.10.20.5

Applications use:

backend-service

5.12 Service vs Pod
              Pod                        Service

 Runs the application        Provides access to the
                             application

 IP changes when             IP remains stable
 recreated

 Temporary                   Permanent until deleted

 Managed by Kubernetes         Routes traffic to Pods

5.13 Advantages of Services
    ●​   Stable network access
    ●​   Automatic load balancing
    ●​   Supports service discovery
    ●​   Easy communication between applications
    ●​   Improves application availability

5.14 Best Practices
    ●​   Use ClusterIP for internal communication.
    ●​   Use NodePort only for development and testing.
    ●​   Use LoadBalancer in production environments.
    ●​   Give meaningful Service names.
    ●​   Verify that the Service selector matches Pod labels.

Real-Time Example
Suppose you deploy an online shopping application.

It contains:

    ●​ Frontend
    ●​ Backend API
    ●​ Database

Communication:

Customer

   |

LoadBalancer Service

   |

Frontend Pods

   |

ClusterIP Service

   |

Backend Pods

   |

ClusterIP Service

   |

Database

Each Service ensures reliable communication even if Pods restart.

Interview Questions
1. What is a Kubernetes Service?

Answer:​
A Service is a Kubernetes resource that provides a stable network endpoint to access one
or more Pods.

2. Why do we need Services?

Answer:​
Pods have temporary IP addresses. Services provide a permanent IP and DNS name,
ensuring reliable communication.

3. What is the default Service type?

Answer:​
ClusterIP.

4. Which Service type exposes an application outside the cluster?

Answer:​
NodePort and LoadBalancer.

5. What is the difference between NodePort and LoadBalancer?

         NodePort                   LoadBalancer

 Uses a port on each          Creates an external IP
 node

 Suitable for testing         Suitable for production

 Manual access                Automatic cloud integration

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Create an Nginx Deployment.

Task 2

Create a ClusterIP Service.

Task 3

Verify the Service using:

kubectl get services

Task 4

Change the Service type to NodePort.

Task 5

Access the application using your browser.

modules.title: Kubernetes Storage
modules.content:
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​ Understand why storage is important in Kubernetes.
   ●​ Learn the difference between temporary and permanent storage.
   ●​ Understand Volumes, Persistent Volumes (PV), Persistent Volume Claims (PVC),
      and Storage Classes.
   ●​ Create and use persistent storage in Kubernetes.

6.1 Introduction to Kubernetes Storage
Applications generate data such as:

   ●​   User information
   ●​   Images
   ●​   Videos
   ●​   Logs
   ●​   Database records

This data should not be lost when an application restarts.

Kubernetes provides Storage to store application data safely.

6.2 Why Do We Need Storage?
Suppose you are running a MySQL database inside a Pod.

The Pod stores customer information.

Now imagine the Pod crashes.

If there is no storage, all customer data is lost.

To prevent this, Kubernetes uses Persistent Storage.

Real-Time Example
Think about your mobile phone.

    ●​ RAM → Temporary memory (data disappears after restart)
    ●​ Internal Storage → Permanent memory (data remains)

Similarly,

    ●​ Pod memory = Temporary
    ●​ Kubernetes Storage = Permanent

6.3 What is a Volume?
A Volume is a storage area attached to a Pod.

It allows containers inside the Pod to store and share data.

Features

    ●​ Shared by all containers in the same Pod.
    ●​ Data remains while the Pod is running.
    ●​ Used for temporary storage.

Simple Diagram

     Pod

  +----------------+

  | Container 1 |

  | Container 2 |

  +----------------+

      |

    Volume

6.4 Types of Volumes
Some commonly used volume types are:

   ●​   emptyDir
   ●​   hostPath
   ●​   configMap
   ●​   secret
   ●​   Persistent Volume (PV)

emptyDir
An emptyDir volume is created when a Pod starts.

   ●​ Data is available while the Pod is running.
   ●​ Data is deleted when the Pod is removed.

Use Case:

   ●​ Temporary files
   ●​ Cache data

hostPath
A hostPath volume stores data on the Worker Node's local disk.

Use Case:

   ●​ Testing
   ●​ Development

Note: Not recommended for production because if the Pod moves to another node, the data
may not be available.

6.5 What is a Persistent Volume (PV)?
A Persistent Volume (PV) is a storage resource created in the Kubernetes cluster.

It exists independently of Pods.

Even if a Pod is deleted, the data stored in the PV remains.

Features

    ●​ Permanent storage
    ●​ Managed by Kubernetes
    ●​ Can be reused by multiple Pods (depending on access mode)

Real-Time Example
Imagine renting a house.

    ●​ The house = Persistent Volume (PV)
    ●​ The tenant = Pod

Even if one tenant leaves, the house still exists.

A new tenant can use the same house.

6.6 What is a Persistent Volume Claim
(PVC)?
A Persistent Volume Claim (PVC) is a request for storage made by a Pod.

Instead of directly using a PV, a Pod requests storage through a PVC.

Flow

Pod

|

PVC (Request)

|

Persistent Volume (PV)

|

Physical Storage

6.7 Persistent Volume Workflow
   1.​ Administrator creates a PV.
   2.​ Application creates a PVC.
   3.​ Kubernetes connects the PVC to a matching PV.
   4.​ The Pod uses the PVC to store data.

This separation makes storage management flexible.

6.8 Storage Class
A Storage Class allows Kubernetes to automatically create storage when a PVC is
requested.

Without a Storage Class:

   ●​ The administrator must manually create PVs.

With a Storage Class:

   ●​ Kubernetes creates the required storage automatically.

Benefits

   ●​ Dynamic provisioning
   ●​ Easier storage management
   ●​ Faster deployments

6.9 Volume YAML Example
apiVersion: v1

kind: Pod

metadata:

 name: nginx-volume

spec:

 containers:

 - name: nginx

  image: nginx

  volumeMounts:

  - mountPath: /data

   name: my-volume

 volumes:

 - name: my-volume

  emptyDir: {}

This example creates a Pod with an emptyDir volume mounted at /data.

6.10 Persistent Volume Claim YAML
apiVersion: v1

kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

metadata:

 name: my-pvc

spec:

 accessModes:

 - ReadWriteOnce

 resources:

  requests:

   storage: 1Gi

Create the PVC:

kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml

6.11 Useful Storage Commands
View Persistent Volumes

kubectl get pv

View Persistent Volume Claims

kubectl get pvc

Describe a PV

kubectl describe pv

Describe a PVC

kubectl describe pvc

Delete a PVC

kubectl delete pvc my-pvc

6.12 PV vs PVC
         Persistent Volume (PV)   Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)

 Actual storage resource          Request for storage

 Created by administrator or Storage       Created by application
 Class

 Exists independently                      Used by Pods

6.13 Advantages of Kubernetes Storage
   ●​   Prevents data loss.
   ●​   Supports persistent applications.
   ●​   Easy storage management.
   ●​   Dynamic provisioning with Storage Classes.
   ●​   Improves application reliability.

6.14 Best Practices
   ●​   Use Persistent Volumes for databases.
   ●​   Avoid using hostPath in production.
   ●​   Use Storage Classes for dynamic provisioning.
   ●​   Regularly back up important data.
   ●​   Monitor storage usage.

Interview Questions
1. What is a Volume in Kubernetes?

Answer: A Volume is a storage area attached to a Pod that allows containers to store and
share data.

2. What is the difference between PV and PVC?

Answer: A Persistent Volume (PV) is the actual storage resource, while a Persistent Volume
Claim (PVC) is a request made by a Pod to use that storage.

3. What is a Storage Class?

Answer: A Storage Class enables Kubernetes to automatically create storage resources
when a PVC requests storage.

4. Which volume type is temporary?

Answer: emptyDir

5. Why should databases use Persistent Volumes?

Answer: Because Persistent Volumes keep data safe even if Pods restart or are recreated.

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Create a Pod with an emptyDir volume.

Task 2

Create a Persistent Volume Claim.

Task 3

Verify the PVC using:

kubectl get pvc

Task 4

Mount the PVC to a Pod.

Task 5

Store a file in the mounted directory and verify that the data remains after restarting the
application (when backed by a Persistent Volume).

modules.title: Configuration Management in
modules.content:
Kubernetes
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Understand Configuration Management in Kubernetes.
   ●​   Learn what ConfigMaps are and why they are used.
   ●​   Understand Kubernetes Secrets.
   ●​   Learn the difference between ConfigMaps and Secrets.
   ●​   Store configuration values without modifying application code.

7.1 Introduction to Configuration
Management
Every application requires some configuration values, such as:

   ●​   Database URL
   ●​   Database Username
   ●​   API URL
   ●​   Server Port
   ●​   Environment Name

Instead of writing these values directly in the application code, Kubernetes stores them
separately using ConfigMaps and Secrets.

Why Configuration Management?
Suppose your application connects to a database.

Database URL:

mysql.company.com

If the database changes, you don't want to modify and rebuild the application.

Instead, you only update the configuration.

This makes applications easier to maintain.

Real-Time Example
Imagine your college ID card.

Your name, branch, and roll number are printed separately from your books.

If your classroom changes, you don't print new books—you simply update the information.

Similarly, Kubernetes stores configuration separately from the application.

7.2 What is a ConfigMap?
A ConfigMap is a Kubernetes object used to store non-sensitive configuration data as
key-value pairs.

Examples:

   ●​   Application Name
   ●​   Database Host
   ●​   API URL
   ●​   Environment
   ●​   Port Number

Example

APP_NAME = Student Portal

PORT = 8080

ENV = Production

The application reads these values from the ConfigMap.

7.3 Why Use ConfigMaps?
Without ConfigMaps:

   ●​ Configuration is hardcoded in the application.

   ●​ Every change requires rebuilding the application.

With ConfigMaps:

   ●​ Update the configuration without changing the application code.
   ●​ Easier deployment across Development, Testing, and Production environments.

7.4 ConfigMap YAML Example
apiVersion: v1

kind: ConfigMap

metadata:

 name: app-config

data:

 APP_NAME: Student Portal

 PORT: "8080"

 ENV: Production

Create the ConfigMap:

kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml

7.5 Viewing ConfigMaps
View all ConfigMaps:

kubectl get configmaps

Describe a ConfigMap:

kubectl describe configmap app-config

Delete a ConfigMap:

kubectl delete configmap app-config

7.6 Using ConfigMap in a Pod
A ConfigMap can be used as:

   ●​ Environment Variables
   ●​ Mounted Files

Example:

env:

- name: APP_NAME

 valueFrom:

  configMapKeyRef:

   name: app-config

   key: APP_NAME

Now the application can access the value using an environment variable.

7.7 What is a Secret?
A Secret is a Kubernetes object used to store sensitive information.

Examples:

   ●​   Database Password
   ●​   API Keys
   ●​   JWT Tokens
   ●​   SSH Keys
   ●​   Certificates

Secrets help protect confidential information instead of storing it directly in YAML files or
source code.

7.8 Why Use Secrets?
Imagine storing your ATM PIN in a public notebook.

Anyone can read it.

Similarly, storing passwords directly in application code is insecure.

Secrets provide a safer way to manage sensitive information.

7.9 Secret YAML Example
apiVersion: v1

kind: Secret

metadata:

 name: db-secret

type: Opaque

stringData:

 username: admin

 password: admin123

Create the Secret:

kubectl apply -f secret.yaml

7.10 Viewing Secrets
View Secrets:

kubectl get secrets

Describe a Secret:

kubectl describe secret db-secret

Delete a Secret:

kubectl delete secret db-secret

7.11 Using Secrets in a Pod
Example:

env:

- name: DB_PASSWORD

 valueFrom:

  secretKeyRef:

   name: db-secret

   key: password

Now the application reads the password from the Secret instead of hardcoding it.

7.12 ConfigMap vs Secret
              ConfigMap                                     Secret

 Stores non-sensitive data          Stores sensitive data

 API URLs, Ports, Environment       Passwords, API Keys, Tokens

 Plain text                         Stored as encoded data (Base64 in Kubernetes
                                    manifests)

 Less secure                      More secure for configuration management

7.13 Best Practices
   ●​    Store passwords in Secrets, not ConfigMaps.
   ●​    Store application settings in ConfigMaps.
   ●​    Avoid hardcoding configuration values in application code.
   ●​    Use different ConfigMaps for Development, Testing, and Production.
   ●​    Restrict access to Secrets using RBAC.

7.14 Real-Time Scenario
A Student Management System has:

   ●​ Database URL
   ●​ Database Username
   ●​ Database Password

Store them as:

ConfigMap

   ●​ Database URL
   ●​ Application Name
   ●​ Environment

Secret

   ●​ Username
   ●​ Password

This keeps the application secure and easy to manage.

Interview Questions
1. What is a ConfigMap?

Answer:​
A ConfigMap is a Kubernetes object used to store non-sensitive configuration data such as
application settings, ports, and API URLs.

2. What is a Secret?

Answer:​
A Secret is a Kubernetes object used to securely store sensitive information like passwords,
API keys, and certificates.

3. What is the difference between ConfigMap and Secret?

Answer:

   ●​ ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration.
   ●​ Secret stores sensitive information securely.

4. Can a Pod use both ConfigMaps and Secrets?

Answer:​
 Yes. A Pod can use ConfigMaps for application settings and Secrets for sensitive
information.

5. Why should passwords not be stored in ConfigMaps?

Answer:​
 Because ConfigMaps are intended for non-sensitive configuration. Passwords should be
stored in Secrets to improve security and follow best practices.

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Create a ConfigMap named app-config.

Task 2

Store:

   ●​ APP_NAME
   ●​ PORT
   ●​ ENV

inside the ConfigMap.

Task 3

Create a Secret named db-secret.

Task 4

Store:

   ●​ username
   ●​ password

inside the Secret.

Task 5

Use both the ConfigMap and Secret in a Pod as environment variables.

modules.title: Advanced Workloads in
modules.content:
Kubernetes
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​    Understand different Kubernetes workload resources.
   ●​    Learn StatefulSets and when to use them.
   ●​    Learn DaemonSets and their purpose.
   ●​    Understand Jobs and CronJobs.
   ●​    Learn about Autoscaling in Kubernetes.

8.1 Introduction to Advanced Workloads
In previous modules, we learned about Pods and Deployments.

However, not every application works the same way.

For example:

    ●​ A Database needs permanent storage.
    ●​ A Monitoring tool should run on every node.
    ●​ A Backup task should run only once every day.

To handle these scenarios, Kubernetes provides Advanced Workloads.

The main workload resources are:

    ●​   StatefulSet
    ●​   DaemonSet
    ●​   Job
    ●​   CronJob
    ●​   Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

8.2 StatefulSet
What is a StatefulSet?
A StatefulSet is a Kubernetes workload used for applications that require:

    ●​ Stable network identity
    ●​ Persistent storage
    ●​ Ordered deployment and scaling

Examples:

    ●​   MySQL
    ●​   PostgreSQL
    ●​   MongoDB
    ●​   Apache Kafka

Why Use StatefulSets?
Imagine you have a MySQL database.

If the Pod restarts:

    ●​ It should keep the same name.
    ●​ It should keep the same storage.

Deployments cannot guarantee this.

StatefulSets can.

Features of StatefulSets
   ●​   Stable Pod names (mysql-0, mysql-1)
   ●​   Persistent storage
   ●​   Ordered creation and deletion
   ●​   Stable network identity

Real-Time Example
A bank database stores customer account details.

Even if the server restarts:

   ●​ Customer data should not be lost.
   ●​ The database should continue from where it stopped.

StatefulSets are ideal for such applications.

8.3 DaemonSet
What is a DaemonSet?
A DaemonSet ensures that one Pod runs on every Worker Node.

Whenever a new Worker Node is added, Kubernetes automatically creates a DaemonSet
Pod on it.

Why Use DaemonSets?
Some applications should run on every server.

Examples:

   ●​   Log Collection
   ●​   Monitoring
   ●​   Security Agents
   ●​   Antivirus Software

Example
Suppose your cluster has 3 Worker Nodes.

Worker Node 1 → Logging Pod

Worker Node 2 → Logging Pod

Worker Node 3 → Logging Pod

If a fourth Worker Node is added:

Worker Node 4 → Logging Pod (Automatically Created)

Common Use Cases
   ●​   Fluentd
   ●​   Prometheus Node Exporter
   ●​   Filebeat
   ●​   Security Monitoring

8.4 Job
What is a Job?
A Job is used to run a task only once.

After the task completes successfully, the Job stops.

Examples
   ●​   Database Backup
   ●​   Data Import
   ●​   Report Generation
   ●​   Image Processing

Real-Time Example
Suppose a company wants to import student data into a database.

The import runs once.

After completion, the Job ends automatically.

8.5 CronJob
What is a CronJob?
A CronJob is used to run tasks automatically at scheduled times.

It works like the Linux cron scheduler.

Examples
   ●​   Daily Backup
   ●​   Weekly Reports
   ●​   Monthly Salary Processing
   ●​   Log Cleanup

Real-Time Example
Every day at 12:00 AM, a company backs up its database.

Instead of manually starting the backup, Kubernetes automatically runs it using a CronJob.

8.6 Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)
What is Autoscaling?
Autoscaling means automatically increasing or decreasing the number of Pods based on
application load.

Kubernetes provides the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA).

How Does HPA Work?
Example:

Normal Traffic

2 Pods

High Traffic

6 Pods

Traffic Decreases

2 Pods

HPA monitors CPU or memory usage and adjusts the number of Pods automatically.

Advantages of Autoscaling
   ●​    Better Performance
   ●​    Lower Cost
   ●​    High Availability
   ●​    Automatic Resource Management

8.7 Comparison of Advanced Workloads

 Resource            Purpose                   Example

Deployment     Stateless               Nginx
               Applications

StatefulSet    Stateful Applications   MySQL

DaemonSet      One Pod per Node        Logging Agent

Job            One-Time Task           Database Import

CronJob        Scheduled Task          Daily Backup

HPA            Automatic Scaling       High-Traffic Website

8.8 Best Practices
   ●​   Use Deployment for web applications.
   ●​   Use StatefulSet for databases.
   ●​   Use DaemonSet for monitoring and logging.
   ●​   Use Job for one-time tasks.
   ●​   Use CronJob for scheduled tasks.
   ●​   Enable HPA for production applications.

Real-Time Scenario
A company runs an e-commerce website.

They use:

   ●​ Deployment → Frontend Website

   ●​   StatefulSet → MySQL Database
   ●​   DaemonSet → Monitoring Agent
   ●​   CronJob → Daily Database Backup
   ●​   HPA → Increase Pods during sales

This combination helps keep the application reliable and scalable.

Interview Questions
1. What is a StatefulSet?

Answer:​
A StatefulSet is a Kubernetes workload used for stateful applications that require stable
network identities and persistent storage.

2. What is a DaemonSet?

Answer:​
A DaemonSet ensures that one Pod runs on every Worker Node in the Kubernetes cluster.

3. What is the difference between a Job and a CronJob?

           Job                    CronJob

 Runs once                 Runs on a schedule

 Used for one-time         Used for recurring
 tasks                     tasks

4. What is HPA?

Answer:​
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically increases or decreases the number of Pods based
on resource usage such as CPU or memory.

5. Which workload is best for databases?

Answer:​
StatefulSet, because it provides stable identities and persistent storage.

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Create a Deployment for an Nginx application.

Task 2

Create a StatefulSet for a MySQL database.

Task 3

Deploy a DaemonSet that runs a monitoring agent on every Worker Node.

Task 4

Create a Job that prints "Hello Kubernetes" once.

Task 5

Create a CronJob that runs every minute and prints the current date.

modules.title: Kubernetes Security
modules.content:
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Understand Kubernetes Security.
   ●​   Learn Authentication and Authorization.
   ●​   Understand RBAC (Role-Based Access Control).
   ●​   Learn Service Accounts.
   ●​   Understand Secrets and Pod Security.
   ●​   Follow Kubernetes security best practices.

9.1 Introduction to Kubernetes Security
Kubernetes clusters contain important resources such as:

   ●​   Applications
   ●​   Databases
   ●​   Secrets
   ●​   Configuration Files
   ●​   User Data

If these resources are not protected, attackers can access or modify them.

Kubernetes provides several security features to protect the cluster.

Why is Security Important?
Imagine a company stores customer banking information in Kubernetes.

If anyone can access the database:

   ●​ Customer information may be stolen.
   ●​ Applications may stop working.
   ●​ Business may suffer huge losses.

Security helps prevent these problems.

Real-Time Example
Think of a college.

   ●​ Students cannot enter the Principal's office anytime.
   ●​ Teachers can access staff rooms.
   ●​ Principal has full access.

Similarly, Kubernetes gives different permissions to different users.

9.2 Authentication

What is Authentication?
Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of a user.

Simple Question:

         Who are you?

Examples:

    ●​      Username and Password
    ●​      Certificates
    ●​      Tokens
    ●​      Cloud IAM Users

If the identity is correct, Kubernetes allows the user to continue.

Example
Prasanna logs into Kubernetes.

The API Server checks the login credentials.

If valid:

Access Granted     ✅
If invalid:

Access Denied     ❌

9.3 Authorization
What is Authorization?
Authorization decides what a user is allowed to do.

Simple Question:

         What are you allowed to do?

Examples:

   ●​ View Pods
   ●​ Create Deployments
   ●​ Delete Services

Different users have different permissions.

Example
Developer:

                   ✅
                    ✅
   ●​ View Pods

                     ❌
   ●​ Create Pods
   ●​ Delete Cluster

Administrator:

   ●​ Full Access   ✅

9.4 RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)
RBAC is a Kubernetes security mechanism that controls access based on roles.

Instead of giving everyone full access, permissions are assigned through roles.

Components of RBAC
   ●​   Role
   ●​   ClusterRole
   ●​   RoleBinding
   ●​   ClusterRoleBinding

Role

A Role provides permissions within a single namespace.

Example:

A developer can:

   ●​ View Pods
   ●​ Create Pods

But cannot access other namespaces.

ClusterRole

A ClusterRole provides permissions across the entire cluster.

Example:

A cluster administrator can manage all namespaces and resources.

RoleBinding

A RoleBinding connects a Role to a user or Service Account.

Example:

Developer → Developer Role

ClusterRoleBinding

A ClusterRoleBinding connects a ClusterRole to users or Service Accounts.

Example:

Administrator → Cluster Admin Role

9.5 Service Accounts
What is a Service Account?
A Service Account is an identity used by applications running inside Kubernetes.

It allows Pods to communicate securely with the Kubernetes API.

Why Use Service Accounts?
Instead of using a human user account, applications use Service Accounts.

Example:

A monitoring application needs to read Pod information.

Instead of giving your personal account, create a Service Account with only the required
permissions.

9.6 Kubernetes Secrets
Secrets store sensitive information such as:

   ●​   Passwords
   ●​   API Keys
   ●​   Certificates
   ●​   Tokens

Never store passwords directly inside application code or public repositories.

9.7 Pod Security
Pod Security protects Pods from running with unsafe configurations.

Examples of good practices:

   ●​   Do not run containers as the root user.
   ●​   Use read-only file systems when possible.
   ●​   Limit Linux capabilities.
   ●​   Define CPU and memory limits.

These practices reduce security risks.

9.8 Network Security
Applications should not communicate with every Pod by default.

Use Network Policies to control traffic.

Example:

Frontend → Backend ✅
Frontend → Database ❌ (Direct access blocked)

This improves security.

9.9 Kubernetes Security Best Practices
   ●​   Use RBAC to control access.
   ●​   Store passwords in Secrets.
   ●​   Use Service Accounts for applications.
   ●​   Keep Kubernetes updated.
   ●​   Limit Pod permissions.
   ●​   Use Network Policies.
   ●​   Regularly monitor cluster activity.
   ●​   Back up important data.

9.10 Common Security Mistakes
❌ Giving everyone cluster-admin access.
❌ Storing passwords in ConfigMaps.
❌ Running containers as the root user.
❌ Ignoring Kubernetes updates.
❌ Allowing unrestricted network communication between Pods.

Real-Time Scenario
A banking application uses Kubernetes.

RBAC

   ●​   Developers → Deploy applications.
   ●​   Database Team → Manage databases.
   ●​   Security Team → View logs and monitor the cluster.
   ●​   Administrator → Full cluster access.

Secrets

   ●​ Database Password
   ●​ API Keys
   ●​ SSL Certificates

Network Policies

   ●​ Customers → Frontend
   ●​ Frontend → Backend
   ●​ Backend → Database

Direct customer access to the database is blocked.

This setup keeps the application secure and follows the principle of least privilege.

Interview Questions
1. What is Authentication?

Answer:​
Authentication verifies the identity of a user or application before allowing access to the
Kubernetes cluster.

2. What is Authorization?

Answer:​
Authorization determines what actions an authenticated user or application is allowed to
perform.

3. What is RBAC?

Answer:​
RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is a Kubernetes security mechanism that grants
permissions based on roles assigned to users or Service Accounts.

4. What is the difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?

              Role                           ClusterRole

 Namespace-specific                   Cluster-wide permissions
 permissions

 Used within one namespace            Used across all
                                      namespaces

5. Why are Service Accounts used?

Answer:​
 Service Accounts provide an identity for applications running inside Kubernetes, allowing
them to securely access the Kubernetes API without using a human user's credentials.

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Create a Service Account named app-service-account.

Task 2

Create a Role that allows reading Pods in a namespace.

Task 3

Bind the Role to the Service Account using a RoleBinding.

Task 4

Create a Secret containing a database password.

Task 5

Verify the created resources using:

kubectl get serviceaccounts

kubectl get roles

kubectl get rolebindings

kubectl get secrets

modules.title: Monitoring & Logging in
modules.content:
Kubernetes
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Understand the importance of Monitoring and Logging.
   ●​   Learn Metrics Server, Prometheus, and Grafana.
   ●​   Understand Logging in Kubernetes.
   ●​   Learn the ELK Stack.
   ●​   Follow monitoring best practices.

10.1 Introduction to Monitoring &
Logging
When an application runs in Kubernetes, we need to know:

   ●​   Is the application running?
   ●​   How much CPU is it using?
   ●​   How much memory is it using?
   ●​   Are there any errors?
   ●​   Why did a Pod crash?

To answer these questions, Kubernetes uses Monitoring and Logging.

What is Monitoring?
Monitoring means continuously checking the health and performance of your Kubernetes
cluster.

Monitoring helps us track:

   ●​   CPU Usage
   ●​   Memory Usage
   ●​   Disk Usage
   ●​   Pod Status
   ●​   Node Health
   ●​   Network Usage

What is Logging?
Logging means collecting and storing application messages.

Logs help developers identify:

   ●​   Errors
   ●​   Warnings
   ●​   User Activities
   ●​   System Events

Real-Time Example
Imagine you are driving a car.

The dashboard shows:

   ●​ Fuel Level
   ●​ Speed
   ●​ Engine Temperature

This is Monitoring.

If the car breaks down, the mechanic checks the service history to find the problem.

This is Logging.

10.2 Metrics Server
What is Metrics Server?

Metrics Server is a lightweight Kubernetes component that collects resource usage
information.

It provides:

    ●​ CPU Usage
    ●​ Memory Usage

Kubernetes uses this information for autoscaling.

Check Resource Usage

View Node usage:

kubectl top nodes

View Pod usage:

kubectl top pods

Advantages
    ●​ Lightweight
    ●​ Easy to install
    ●​ Supports Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

10.3 Prometheus
What is Prometheus?
Prometheus is an open-source monitoring tool used to collect and store metrics from
Kubernetes.

It automatically collects information such as:

    ●​   CPU Usage
    ●​   Memory Usage
    ●​   Network Usage
    ●​   Pod Status
    ●​   Node Health

Features
   ●​   Time-series database
   ●​   Alerting
   ●​   Powerful queries
   ●​   Easy integration with Kubernetes

Real-Time Example
A hospital monitors:

   ●​ Heart Rate
   ●​ Blood Pressure
   ●​ Oxygen Level

Similarly, Prometheus continuously monitors the health of Kubernetes.

10.4 Grafana
What is Grafana?
Grafana is a visualization tool used to display monitoring data in dashboards.

Grafana works with Prometheus to create charts and graphs.

What Can Grafana Display?
   ●​   CPU Usage Graph
   ●​   Memory Usage Graph
   ●​   Pod Status
   ●​   Node Status
   ●​   Disk Usage
   ●​   Network Traffic

Why Use Grafana?
Instead of reading numbers, Grafana presents information in an easy-to-understand
dashboard.

10.5 Logging in Kubernetes
Applications generate logs while running.

Logs help us:

   ●​   Find errors
   ●​   Debug applications
   ●​   Monitor user requests
   ●​   Troubleshoot problems

View Pod Logs
kubectl logs <pod-name>

Example:

kubectl logs nginx-pod

Follow Live Logs
kubectl logs -f nginx-pod

The -f option displays logs in real time.

10.6 ELK Stack
The ELK Stack is a popular logging solution.

ELK stands for:

   ●​ E → Elasticsearch

   ●​ L → Logstash
   ●​ K → Kibana

Elasticsearch
Stores and indexes log data for fast searching.

Logstash
Collects logs from applications and sends them to Elasticsearch.

Kibana
Displays logs using dashboards and charts.

ELK Workflow
Application

   |

 Logstash

   |

Elasticsearch

   |

 Kibana Dashboard

10.7 Monitoring Tools Comparison

        Tool                   Purpose

 Metrics Server    CPU & Memory Metrics

 Prometheus        Monitoring & Metrics Collection

 Grafana           Visualization Dashboard

 ELK Stack         Log Collection & Analysis

10.8 Best Practices
   ●​    Monitor all Worker Nodes.
   ●​    Enable alerts for high CPU or memory usage.
   ●​    Store logs securely.
   ●​    Delete old logs regularly.
   ●​    Use dashboards to track application health.
   ●​    Monitor both applications and infrastructure.

10.9 Common Monitoring Problems
High CPU Usage

Reason: Heavy application traffic.

Solution: Enable Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA).

High Memory Usage

Reason: Memory leaks or large workloads.

Solution: Set memory limits and optimize the application.

Missing Logs

Reason: Logging agent not configured correctly.

Solution: Verify the logging setup and ensure logs are being collected.

Real-Time Scenario
An e-commerce website is running on Kubernetes.

The DevOps team uses:

   ●​   Metrics Server → Check CPU and memory usage.
   ●​   Prometheus → Monitor Pods and Nodes.
   ●​   Grafana → Display dashboards.
   ●​   ELK Stack → Collect application logs.

When CPU usage increases during a sale, HPA automatically creates more Pods. If an
application crashes, the team checks logs in Kibana to identify the cause.

Interview Questions
1. What is Monitoring?

Answer:​
Monitoring is the process of continuously checking the health, performance, and resource
usage of a Kubernetes cluster.

2. What is Logging?

Answer:​
 Logging is the process of collecting and storing application and system logs to help
troubleshoot issues.

3. What is Prometheus?

Answer:​
 Prometheus is an open-source monitoring tool that collects metrics from Kubernetes and
stores them in a time-series database.

4. What is Grafana?

Answer:​
 Grafana is a visualization tool used to create dashboards and graphs from monitoring data
collected by tools like Prometheus.

5. What does ELK stand for?

Answer:

   ●​ Elasticsearch
   ●​ Logstash
   ●​ Kibana

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Install the Metrics Server.

Task 2

Run:

kubectl top nodes

Task 3

Run:

kubectl top pods

Task 4

modules.title: Helm – Kubernetes Package
modules.content:
Manager
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Understand what Helm is.
   ●​   Learn why Helm is used in Kubernetes.
   ●​   Understand Helm Charts.
   ●​   Install applications using Helm.
   ●​   Learn basic Helm commands.
   ●​   Follow Helm best practices.

11.1 Introduction to Helm
Imagine you want to install a complex application like WordPress on Kubernetes.

Without Helm:

   ●​   Create Deployment YAML
   ●​   Create Service YAML
   ●​   Create ConfigMap
   ●​   Create Secret
   ●​   Create Persistent Volume
   ●​   Create Persistent Volume Claim
   ●​   Configure everything manually

This process is time-consuming and error-prone.

Helm simplifies this process.

What is Helm?
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes.

It helps you install, update, and manage Kubernetes applications using pre-configured
packages called Helm Charts.

Simple Definition

         Helm is a tool that simplifies the deployment and management of applications in
         Kubernetes.

Real-Time Example
Think about your smartphone.

Instead of downloading each file separately, you install an app from the Play Store.

The Play Store downloads and installs everything automatically.

Similarly:

    ●​ Play Store → Helm
    ●​ App → Helm Chart
    ●​ Phone → Kubernetes Cluster

11.2 Why Do We Need Helm?
Without Helm:

    ●​    Many YAML files
    ●​    Manual configuration
    ●​    Difficult updates
    ●​    Difficult rollbacks

With Helm:

    ●​    One command installation
    ●​    Easy upgrades
    ●​    Easy rollback
    ●​    Reusable templates
    ●​    Faster deployments

11.3 What is a Helm Chart?
A Helm Chart is a package that contains all the Kubernetes resources required to deploy an
application.

A chart may include:

   ●​   Deployment
   ●​   Service
   ●​   ConfigMap
   ●​   Secret
   ●​   Ingress
   ●​   Persistent Volume
   ●​   Persistent Volume Claim

Instead of managing multiple YAML files, Helm manages everything together.

11.4 Helm Architecture
         Developer

            |

          Helm CLI

            |

        Kubernetes API

            |

        Kubernetes Cluster

            |

         Helm Chart

Image Suggestion: Search "Helm Architecture Diagram" and insert it here.

11.5 Installing Helm
Step 1

Download Helm from the official Helm website.

Step 2

Install Helm.

Step 3

Verify the installation.

helm version

Example Output:

version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.x.x"}

11.6 Searching Helm Charts
Search available charts:

helm search hub nginx

Search repositories:

helm search repo nginx

These commands display available Helm Charts.

11.7 Installing an Application
Install Nginx using Helm.

helm install my-nginx bitnami/nginx

Where:

    ●​ my-nginx → Release Name
    ●​ bitnami/nginx → Chart Name

Verify installation:

helm list

11.8 Upgrading an Application
Suppose a new version of Nginx is available.

Upgrade using:

helm upgrade my-nginx bitnami/nginx

Helm updates the application without reinstalling it.

11.9 Rolling Back an Application
If an upgrade causes problems, return to the previous version.

helm rollback my-nginx 1

Here:

    ●​ 1 = Previous revision number.

Rollback is one of Helm's most useful features.

11.10 Uninstalling an Application
Remove the application.

helm uninstall my-nginx

Helm deletes all resources created by that release.

11.11 Important Helm Commands

Check Helm Version

helm version

List Releases

helm list

Search Charts

helm search repo nginx

Install Chart

helm install my-app chart-name

Upgrade Chart

helm upgrade my-app chart-name

Rollback Release

helm rollback my-app 1

Uninstall Release

helm uninstall my-app

11.12 Advantages of Helm
    ●​   Easy application deployment.
    ●​   Faster installations.
    ●​   Easy upgrades.
    ●​   Easy rollback.
    ●​   Reusable templates.
    ●​   Simplified Kubernetes management.

11.13 Best Practices
    ●​   Use trusted Helm repositories.
    ●​   Test upgrades before production.
    ●​   Use meaningful release names.
    ●​   Store custom configuration in values.yaml.

   ●​ Keep Helm updated.

11.14 Common Mistakes
❌ Editing chart files directly after installation.
❌ Installing untrusted charts.
❌ Forgetting to back up application data before upgrades.
❌ Not checking release history before rollback.

Real-Time Scenario
A company wants to deploy WordPress.

Without Helm:

   ●​ 15+ YAML files
   ●​ Manual deployment
   ●​ Complex updates

With Helm:

helm install wordpress bitnami/wordpress

Within a few minutes, WordPress is deployed with all required Kubernetes resources.

This saves time and reduces configuration errors.

Interview Questions
1. What is Helm?

Answer:​
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes used to install, upgrade, manage, and remove
Kubernetes applications.

2. What is a Helm Chart?

Answer:​
A Helm Chart is a package containing Kubernetes resource definitions required to deploy an
application.

3. What is a Release in Helm?

Answer:​
A Release is an installed instance of a Helm Chart running in a Kubernetes cluster.

4. Which command installs a Helm Chart?

helm install my-app chart-name

5. Which command rolls back a release?

helm rollback my-app 1

modules.title: CI/CD with Kubernetes
modules.content:
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Understand CI/CD concepts.
   ●​   Learn how Kubernetes fits into a CI/CD pipeline.
   ●​   Understand Jenkins, GitHub Actions, and Argo CD.
   ●​   Learn Rolling Updates and Rollbacks.
   ●​   Understand a real-world deployment workflow.

12.1 Introduction to CI/CD
When developers build an application, they continuously make changes by adding new
features, fixing bugs, or improving performance.

Deploying these changes manually every time is slow and can lead to errors.

To automate this process, companies use CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous
Deployment/Delivery).

What is CI?
Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of automatically building and testing code
whenever developers push changes to a repository.

CI Process

   1.​ Developer writes code.
   2.​ Code is pushed to GitHub.
   3.​ CI tool automatically builds the application.
   4.​ Automated tests are executed.
   5.​ If all tests pass, the application is ready for deployment.

Popular CI Tools:

   ●​ Jenkins
   ●​ GitHub Actions
   ●​ GitLab CI

What is CD?

Continuous Deployment/Continuous Delivery (CD) automatically deploys tested
applications to servers or Kubernetes clusters.

Benefits:

   ●​   Faster software delivery.
   ●​   Fewer manual errors.
   ●​   Easy updates.
   ●​   Quick bug fixes.

12.2 CI/CD Pipeline
A typical Kubernetes CI/CD pipeline looks like this:

Developer

   |

Push Code to GitHub

   |

CI Tool (Jenkins / GitHub Actions)

   |

Build Docker Image

   |

Push Image to Docker Hub

   |

Deploy to Kubernetes

   |

Users Access Application

This pipeline automates the complete software delivery process.

12.3 Jenkins

What is Jenkins?
Jenkins is an open-source automation server used to build, test, and deploy applications.

Features

   ●​   Automates software builds.
   ●​   Runs automated tests.
   ●​   Builds Docker images.
   ●​   Deploys applications to Kubernetes.
   ●​   Supports thousands of plugins.

Example Workflow

Developer pushes code → Jenkins detects the change → Builds Docker image → Pushes
image to Docker Hub → Deploys to Kubernetes.

12.4 GitHub Actions
What is GitHub Actions?
GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in automation service.

It can automatically:

   ●​   Build applications.
   ●​   Run tests.
   ●​   Build Docker images.
   ●​   Deploy applications.

Advantages

   ●​ No separate Jenkins server required.
   ●​ Easy integration with GitHub.
   ●​ Simple YAML-based workflow configuration.

12.5 Argo CD
What is Argo CD?

Argo CD is a GitOps continuous deployment tool for Kubernetes.

It continuously monitors a Git repository.

Whenever configuration files change, Argo CD automatically updates the Kubernetes cluster.

Benefits

   ●​    Automatic synchronization.
   ●​    Easy rollback.
   ●​    Git as the single source of truth.
   ●​    Better deployment visibility.

12.6 Rolling Updates
What is a Rolling Update?
A Rolling Update updates an application without downtime.

Instead of stopping all Pods at once, Kubernetes replaces them one by one.

Example

Before Update:

Pod v1

Pod v1

Pod v1

After Update:

Pod v2

Pod v2

Pod v2

Users can continue using the application while the update is happening.

12.7 Rollbacks

What is a Rollback?
If a new version has problems, Kubernetes can return to the previous working version.

Example

   ●​ Version 1.0 → Working
   ●​ Version 2.0 → Contains a bug

Rollback restores Version 1.0 quickly, reducing downtime.

12.8 Benefits of CI/CD
   ●​   Faster software releases.
   ●​   Automatic testing.
   ●​   Fewer deployment errors.
   ●​   Improved software quality.
   ●​   Easy rollback.
   ●​   Better team collaboration.

12.9 Best Practices
   ●​   Store source code in Git.
   ●​   Run automated tests before deployment.
   ●​   Use versioned Docker images.
   ●​   Use Rolling Updates to avoid downtime.
   ●​   Monitor deployments after every release.
   ●​   Keep CI/CD pipelines simple and secure.

12.10 Common Mistakes
❌ Deploying directly to production without testing.
❌ Using the latest Docker image tag for production.
❌ Ignoring failed pipeline tests.
❌ Not maintaining version control.

❌ Skipping rollback planning.

Real-Time Scenario
A company develops an online shopping application.

   1.​ A developer writes new code.
   2.​ The code is pushed to GitHub.
   3.​ GitHub Actions automatically builds the project.
   4.​ A Docker image is created.
   5.​ The image is pushed to Docker Hub.
   6.​ Kubernetes deploys the new version.
   7.​ Rolling Update replaces old Pods one by one.
   8.​ If a problem occurs, Kubernetes performs a Rollback.

This process allows the company to release updates quickly and safely.

Interview Questions
1. What is CI?

Answer:​
Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of automatically building and testing code
whenever developers commit changes.

2. What is CD?

Answer:​
Continuous Deployment/Delivery (CD) is the process of automatically deploying tested
applications to production or other environments.

3. What is Jenkins?

Answer:​
Jenkins is an open-source automation server used to build, test, and deploy applications.

4. What is GitHub Actions?

Answer:​
GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in automation platform used to create CI/CD workflows
directly from a GitHub repository.

5. What is the difference between a Rolling Update and a Rollback?

             Rolling Update                                     Rollback

 Deploys a new version gradually without      Restores the previous stable version if the new
 downtime                                     version fails

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Create a GitHub repository.

Task 2

Build a Docker image for a sample application.

Task 3

Push the Docker image to Docker Hub.

Task 4

Deploy the image to a Kubernetes cluster.

Task 5

Update the application and observe a Rolling Update.

Task 6

Perform a Rollback to the previous version.

modules.title: Troubleshooting Kubernetes
modules.content:
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Understand Kubernetes troubleshooting.
   ●​   Learn common kubectl commands.
   ●​   Debug Pods and Deployments.
   ●​   Analyze logs and events.
   ●​   Solve common Kubernetes issues.
   ●​   Follow troubleshooting best practices.

13.1 Introduction to Troubleshooting
No application runs perfectly all the time. Sometimes:

   ●​   Pods fail to start.
   ●​   Containers crash.
   ●​   Services become unavailable.
   ●​   Applications become slow.

Troubleshooting is the process of identifying, analyzing, and fixing these problems.

Why is Troubleshooting Important?
Imagine an online shopping website.

During a sale:

   ●​ Website stops responding.
   ●​ Customers cannot place orders.

The DevOps team must quickly identify the problem and restore the application.

Kubernetes provides several tools and commands to troubleshoot such issues.

Real-Time Example

Think of a doctor treating a patient.

   1.​ Check symptoms.
   2.​ Find the cause.
   3.​ Give treatment.

Similarly, in Kubernetes:

   1.​ Check Pod status.
   2.​ View logs.
   3.​ Find the issue.
   4.​ Fix the problem.

13.2 Useful kubectl Commands
View Nodes

kubectl get nodes

Shows all Worker Nodes in the cluster.

View Pods

kubectl get pods

Lists all running Pods.

View Deployments

kubectl get deployments

Displays all Deployments.

View Services

kubectl get services

Shows available Services.

View Namespaces

kubectl get namespaces

Displays all Namespaces.

13.3 Describe a Resource
To get detailed information about a Pod:

kubectl describe pod nginx-pod

This command shows:

   ●​   Pod status
   ●​   Events
   ●​   Errors
   ●​   Container details
   ●​   Resource information

It is one of the first commands used during troubleshooting.

13.4 Checking Logs
Application logs help identify runtime errors.

View logs:

kubectl logs nginx-pod

Follow live logs:

kubectl logs -f nginx-pod

Logs may show errors such as:

   ●​   Database connection failed.
   ●​   File not found.
   ●​   Permission denied.
   ●​   Application crashed.

13.5 Debugging Pods
If a Pod is not running:

Step 1

Check Pod status.

kubectl get pods

Example:

STATUS = CrashLoopBackOff

Step 2

Describe the Pod.

kubectl describe pod nginx-pod

Step 3

View logs.

kubectl logs nginx-pod

Step 4

Fix the issue and redeploy.

13.6 Common Pod Status
         Status                    Meaning

 Running                   Pod is working normally

 Pending               Waiting for resources

 CrashLoopBackOff      Container keeps crashing

 Error                 Application failed

 Completed             Task finished successfully

13.7 Common Kubernetes Errors
ImagePullBackOff
Reason

The Docker image cannot be downloaded.

Solution

   ●​ Check image name.
   ●​ Verify Docker Hub repository.
   ●​ Ensure internet access.

CrashLoopBackOff
Reason

The application starts but crashes repeatedly.

Solution

   ●​ Check application logs.
   ●​ Verify configuration.
   ●​ Fix application errors.

Pending
Reason

No available resources.

Solution

    ●​ Add Worker Nodes.
    ●​ Reduce resource requests.
    ●​ Check Scheduler events.

ErrImagePull
Reason

Image does not exist or access is denied.

Solution

Verify:

    ●​ Image name
    ●​ Image tag
    ●​ Registry credentials

13.8 Events
Events provide information about cluster activities.

View events:

kubectl get events

Events show:

    ●​    Pod creation
    ●​    Scheduling
    ●​    Failures
    ●​    Resource issues

13.9 Resource Usage
Check CPU and Memory usage.

kubectl top nodes

Check Pod usage.

kubectl top pods

These commands help identify overloaded applications.

13.10 Best Practices
   ●​   Always check Pod status first.
   ●​   Read logs carefully.
   ●​   Use describe before making changes.
   ●​   Monitor CPU and memory usage.
   ●​   Keep Kubernetes components updated.
   ●​   Use meaningful Pod and Deployment names.

13.11 Common Troubleshooting
Workflow
Application Problem

    │

    ▼

Check Pod Status

    │

    ▼

Describe Pod

     │

     ▼

View Logs

     │

     ▼

Check Events

     │

     ▼

Fix Issue

     │

     ▼

Verify Application

Real-Time Scenario
A company deploys an online shopping application.

Problem:

Customers report that the website is not loading.

The DevOps engineer performs the following steps:

   1.​ Runs kubectl get pods.
   2.​ Finds the Pod in CrashLoopBackOff state.
   3.​ Runs kubectl logs to view the error.
   4.​ Discovers a wrong database password.
   5.​ Updates the Secret.
   6.​ Restarts the Deployment.

The application starts working again.

Interview Questions
1. Which command displays all Pods?

kubectl get pods

2. Which command shows detailed Pod information?

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

3. Which command displays Pod logs?

kubectl logs <pod-name>

4. What is CrashLoopBackOff?

Answer:

CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts but repeatedly crashes due to an application
or configuration issue.

5. What is ImagePullBackOff?

Answer:

ImagePullBackOff occurs when Kubernetes cannot download the required container image
from the registry.

Practical Exercise
Task 1

Deploy an Nginx Pod.

Task 2

Check the Pod status.

kubectl get pods

Task 3

View Pod details.

kubectl describe pod nginx

Task 4

Check application logs.

kubectl logs nginx

Task 5

Delete the Pod and observe Kubernetes creating a new Pod (if managed by a Deployment).

modules.content:
Preparation & Cheat Sheet
Learning Objectives
After completing this module, you will be able to:

   ●​   Prepare for Kubernetes interviews.
   ●​   Revise important Kubernetes concepts.
   ●​   Learn frequently asked interview questions.
   ●​   Practice important kubectl commands.
   ●​   Follow interview preparation tips.

15.1 Kubernetes Interview Preparation
Kubernetes interviews generally contain three rounds:

1. Theory Round

The interviewer asks Kubernetes concepts.

Examples:

   ●​ What is Kubernetes?
   ●​ What is a Pod?
   ●​ What is a Deployment?

2. Practical Round

The interviewer asks you to perform Kubernetes tasks.

Examples:

   ●​ Create a Pod.
   ●​ Expose a Service.
   ●​ Check Pod logs.

   ●​ Deploy an application.

3. Scenario-Based Round

The interviewer gives a real-world problem.

Example:

      "Your Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff state. What will you do?"

Expected answer:

   1.​ Check Pod status.
   2.​ Describe the Pod.
   3.​ View logs.
   4.​ Identify the error.
   5.​ Fix the issue.

15.2 Frequently Asked Interview
Questions
1. What is Kubernetes?

Answer:

Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform used to deploy, manage,
scale, and monitor containerized applications.

2. What is a Pod?

Answer:

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It contains one or more containers that
share the same network and storage.

3. What is a Deployment?

Answer:

A Deployment manages Pods and ensures the desired number of Pods are always running.
It also supports rolling updates and rollbacks.

4. What is a Service?

Answer:

A Service provides a stable network endpoint that allows users or other applications to
access Pods.

5. What is the difference between a Pod and a Deployment?

             Pod                        Deployment

 Runs one or more               Manages Pods
 containers

 Temporary                      Ensures desired state

 Can fail without recovery      Automatically recreates
                                Pods

6. What is a ConfigMap?

Answer:

A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration data such as application settings and
environment variables.

7. What is a Secret?

Answer:

A Secret stores sensitive information such as passwords, API keys, and certificates.

8. What is Helm?

Answer:

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes that simplifies application deployment using
Helm Charts.

9. What is StatefulSet?

Answer:

A StatefulSet is used for stateful applications like databases that require stable identities and
persistent storage.

10. What is a DaemonSet?

Answer:

A DaemonSet ensures that one Pod runs on every Worker Node in the cluster.

15.3 Scenario-Based Questions
Scenario 1

A Pod is in Pending state.

Possible Reasons:

   ●​ Insufficient CPU or Memory.
   ●​ No available Worker Node.
   ●​ Scheduling issue.

Solution:

   ●​ Check node resources.
   ●​ View events using:

kubectl get events

Scenario 2

Application is not accessible.

Check:

   ●​   Pod Status
   ●​   Service
   ●​   Ports
   ●​   Labels
   ●​   Network Policies

Scenario 3

Container keeps restarting.

Reason:

CrashLoopBackOff.

Solution:

kubectl logs <pod-name>

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

View Nodes

kubectl get nodes

View Pods

kubectl get pods

View Services

kubectl get svc

View Deployments

kubectl get deployments

Describe Pod

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

View Logs

kubectl logs <pod-name>

Delete Pod

kubectl delete pod <pod-name>

Apply YAML

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

Delete Resource

kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml

                     <pod-name>

                      <pod-name>

15.6 Kubernetes Best Practices
   ●​   Use Deployments instead of standalone Pods.
   ●​   Store passwords in Secrets.

   ●​   Use Persistent Volumes for databases.
   ●​   Monitor CPU and Memory usage.
   ●​   Keep Kubernetes updated.
   ●​   Use namespaces to organize applications.
   ●​   Test changes before deploying to production.

15.7 Common Mistakes
❌ Running applications without resource limits.
❌ Using the latest Docker image tag in production.
❌ Storing passwords inside application code.
❌ Ignoring Pod logs during troubleshooting.
❌ Deploying directly to production without testing.

      Pod to maintain the desired state.
   ●​ If it is a standalone Pod, Kubernetes does not recreate it automatically.
